    An Interactive Table

    Last updated on 2026-11-19 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 21 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do you build a summary table of OA indicators per publisher?
    • How do you display it as an interactive, searchable table with the DT package?
    • How do you adapt the table display?

    Objectives

    • Create a summary table of publications and OA share per publisher
    • Display a data frame as an interactive table with datatable()
    • Adjust the table with arguments such as rownames, colnames and filter
    • Remove rows with missing values with filter() and is.na()

    Why an interactive table?

    A static table answers the questions you thought of in advance. An interactive table lets the people who use the dashboard explore the data on their own: a colleague handling the APC payments can search for one publisher or sort by the OA share. In a Quarto dashboard this needs no extra server, instead interactive elements can run directly in the user’s browser.

    In this episode we fill the second page of the dashboard, “Publications”, with an interactive table.

    A summary table per publisher

    The table is only as useful as the data it displays. A useful overview for OA monitoring could be one row per publisher with the number of publications, the number of OA publications and the OA share.

    To create such a table we will use some of the functions from the previous episodes: group_by() + summarise(), sum() and mean() applied to the is_oa column, and arrange().

    R 

    oa_by_publisher <- oa_df |>
  group_by(publisher) |>
  summarise(
    publications = n(),
    oa_publications = sum(is_oa),
    oa_share = round(mean(is_oa) * 100, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(publications))

oa_by_publisher

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 44 × 4
   publisher                       publications oa_publications oa_share
   <chr>                                  <int>           <int>    <dbl>
 1 Wiley                                   2566            2196     85.6
 2 Springer Science+Business Media         1294            1166     90.1
 3 Elsevier BV                              470             354     75.3
 4 Nature Portfolio                         394             378     95.9
 5 BioMed Central                           256             256    100
 6 Springer Nature                          214             204     95.3
 7 American Chemical Society                124             108     87.1
 8 Cambridge University Press                97              79     81.4
 9 Royal Society of Chemistry                86              85     98.8
10 Springer VS                               52              50     96.2
# ℹ 34 more rows

    summarise() can calculate several values at once: separate them with commas. The n() function counts the rows in each group, and desc() inside arrange() sorts the largest number of publications first.

    An interactive table with DT

    The DT package turns a data frame into an interactive table, with sorting, searching and paging built in. We already loaded the package with library(DT) in our setup chunk at the top of our dashboard:

    R 

    #| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(DT)

my_ror <- "https://ror.org/01y9bpm73"

oa_all <- read_csv("data/jct_oal_TA_dataset.csv")

oa_df <- oa_all |>
  filter(ror == my_ror) |>
  mutate(is_oa = oa_status != "closed")

    Now we will replace the placeholder chunk on the “Publications” page. We want the chunk to calculate the summary table and pass it to the datatable() function from the DT package:

    R 

    #| title: "Publications by Publisher"

oa_by_publisher <- oa_df |>
  group_by(publisher) |>
  summarise(
    publications = n(),
    oa_publications = sum(is_oa),
    oa_share = round(mean(is_oa) * 100, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(publications))

datatable(oa_by_publisher)

    Render the dashboard and switch to the “Publications” page. Click a column header to sort or type into the search box to test out the functionalities.

    The default table is already useful, but datatable() has arguments to adapt its display:

    R 

    datatable(
  oa_by_publisher,
  rownames = FALSE,
  colnames = c("Publisher", "Publications", "OA publications", "OA share (%)"),
  filter = "top"
)
    • rownames = FALSE removes the row numbers
    • colnames sets readable column headers, in the same order as the columns
    • filter = "top" adds a filter field above each column

    Notice the structure: arguments inside datatable() are separated by commas. Replace your datatable(oa_by_publisher) line with this version and render again.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Missing publishers

    The budget office wants to use the publisher overview for the annual OA report. But some articles have no publisher in the data: in R, a missing value is written NA, and in our table these articles are summed up in one row with an empty publisher field. The function is.na() tests whether a value is missing: it returns TRUE for every NA.

    1. How many articles in oa_df have no publisher?
    2. Change the code of your table, so that these articles are left out.

    The exclamation mark ! turns TRUE into FALSE and the other way round. Use both inside filter() to keep only the rows where the publisher is not missing. Do this before group_by().

    1. sum() of the TRUE/FALSE values counts how many articles have no publisher:

    R 

    sum(is.na(oa_df$publisher))
    1. Add a filter() step before group_by():

    R 

    oa_by_publisher <- oa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(publisher)) |>
  group_by(publisher) |>
  summarise(
    publications = n(),
    oa_publications = sum(is_oa),
    oa_share = round(mean(is_oa) * 100, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(publications))

    In the dashboard, add the same filter(!is.na(publisher)) line to the chunk on the “Publications” page.

    Key Points

    • Prepare the data frame first (group_by() + summarise() + arrange()), then display it
    • DT::datatable() turns a data frame into a sortable, searchable table
    • Arguments like rownames, colnames and filter adapt the table appearance
    • is.na() finds missing values; filter(!is.na(column)) removes them
